ARG.story:
During the military dictatorship that ruled Argentina from 1976 to 1983, the armed and security forces held people in secret detention camps, and some of the women held there were pregnant. Their babies, and children kidnapped with their parents, were given to military families and allies of the regime and registered as those families' own children.

In 1977 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo was founded to find these children. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data, which holds relatives' DNA for matching. In December 1983 President Raúl Alfonsín set up the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, known as CONADEP. Its 1984 report, Nunca Más, recorded 8,960 forced disappearances and at least 200 children under 15 kidnapped. In 2012 a federal court in Buenos Aires found that the junta, the ruling group of military commanders, had run a "systematic plan" to take children born to detained or disappeared mothers. It sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years and Reynaldo Bignone to 15. About 500 children are estimated to have been taken, and by July 2025 the Grandmothers had identified 140 of them.

The Italian priest Nicola Corradi had been accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese there in 2011, and he went on working at the order's school in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza. In 2019 a Mendoza court convicted him, the priest Horacio Corbacho and a gardener of abusing children there between 2004 and 2016, with sentences of 42, 45 and 18 years.

In Tucumán, a young woman was allegedly abducted in 2002 into forced prostitution by a brothel and trafficking network that also trafficked minors. The trial over her case ended in 2012 with all 13 defendants acquitted. The province's Supreme Court reversed this in 2013 and found 10 of them guilty. Campaigners and the family's lawyers said police were often paid to protect such networks.

Most of the children taken under the dictatorship have still not been identified, and the search for them continues through DNA matching.

BGD.story:
Between 1967 and 1997/98, children from Bangladesh were among those adopted by families in the Netherlands. In 2021 a Dutch government commission chaired by Tjibbe Joustra found "serious violations" in adoptions from several countries, including Bangladesh, and concluded that the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses. The Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption the same year.

The US State Department publishes a yearly report on how each country deals with human trafficking. Its 2025 report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in sex trafficking abroad, including in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate that children are 40 per cent of the Bangladeshi victims exploited abroad. The report also says tourists have increased demand for the sexual exploitation of girls near Cox's Bazar, including Rohingya girls. More than one million Rohingya refugees live there in 33 camps. In neighbouring Myanmar, a UN fact-finding mission found that the armed forces raped hundreds of Rohingya women and girls during "clearance operations" in 2017.

The report names corruption and official complicity as significant concerns, including corrupt policing in the Rohingya camps. In the period the report covers, courts convicted 103 traffickers, down from 407.

Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates of child sexual exploitation, found in 2026 that South Asia lacks representative survey data on abuse carried out through technology.

Bangladeshi girls are still trafficked abroad and exploited near the camps, and fewer traffickers are being convicted. How many Bangladeshi children are abused online is not known.

CHE.story:
Mainly from 1930 to 1981, Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities sent more than 60,000 people to about 650 institutions without any court order, a practice known as administrative detention. They included the Verdingkinder, children placed with farmers as indentured labourers. People held in these institutions were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. A programme of the foundation Pro Juventute, backed by federal authorities, removed about 590 Yenish children from their families.

The Swiss government apologised in 2010. A 2016 law gave victims of these compulsory measures a "solidarity contribution" of CHF 25,000, and in 2019 an independent expert commission set up by federal law published its final report. In February 2025 the government recognised the Pro Juventute programme as a crime against humanity.

From the 1970s, Swiss families adopted children from abroad, including 1,111 from South Korea between 1968 and 1997 and others from Sri Lanka, India and Tibet. Swiss authorities realised that many of these children had been wrongly presented as orphans, and that the placements were driven by money and linked to organised child trafficking. Decisions often rested on incomplete or falsified documents. After pressure from adoptees' groups such as Back to the Roots, parliament commissioned a study in 2018. The Federal Council, the Swiss government, acknowledged the authorities' failures in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

In 2023 historians at the University of Zurich, in a study paid for by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders, documented 1,002 cases of sexual abuse in the Catholic Church since 1950, with 510 accused people and 921 victims. Of the documents, 74 percent concerned minors, and about 30 percent of cases took place in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers found that church law was hardly ever applied and that many cases were kept secret.

The state has apologised to and paid victims of the forced placements, and the government has proposed ending intercountry adoption. The church researchers said the cases they found were only a small part of the total, so the full number of children abused in the church is not known.

COL.story:
In 1981 the New York Times reported that Colombian authorities had found a ring in which hundreds of poor children from the Andes were taken or bought from their mothers and sold abroad for adoption with forged papers. Adoptions continued, and from 1994 to 2014 the United States issued 5,519 immigrant visas to children adopted from Bogotá. Colombia still sends children abroad, and 20,864 left for adoption between 2003 and 2022.

During the armed conflict, guerrilla groups, paramilitaries and the state security forces recruited children. In 2022 the Truth Commission, set up to establish what happened in the conflict, documented 16,238 children recruited between 1990 and 2017 and estimated the real number at 27,101 to 40,828. It found that recruited girls were forced to use contraception and to have abortions, and were raped. The Special Jurisdiction for Peace, the court that tries crimes of the conflict, has indicted former commanders of the FARC-EP guerrilla group for recruiting children and for sexual violence against them. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 33 girls by armed groups still operating, including the ELN guerrilla group, groups that broke away from the FARC-EP, and the Clan del Golfo.

Girls are also sold for sex. The 2025 US State Department report on trafficking says this is common in tourist areas and in places where natural resources are extracted, and that the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua moves victims through Cúcuta. By May 2026 US courts had sentenced 10 American men for exploiting children in Medellín; one had entered the city 48 times in two years.

Colombia has held no national inquiry into abuse in its institutions. In 2020 the Constitutional Court ordered the Archdiocese of Medellín to give a journalist, Juan Pablo Barrientos, the records of accused priests, and in 2022 agreed to review a request covering 915 priests.

Armed groups and criminal networks continue to abuse and sell girls in Colombia. How many children were abused in church institutions is unknown, because the archdiocese has not fully complied with the court.

ESP.story:
From 1939 the Franco regime held its Republican opponents in prison, among them mothers. A 1940 law let imprisoned mothers keep their children only until the age of three, after which the state took custody, and by 1943 there were 12,043 Republican children in state care. The regime's welfare bodies, Auxilio Social and the Women's Protection Board, removed about 30,000 children of Republican prisoners, and some were given new names so they could be handed to families loyal to the regime. In 2008 Judge Baltasar Garzón of the Audiencia Nacional, Spain's national criminal court, called these removals crimes against humanity.

The taking of babies from confined women went on into the early 1980s. In 2011 the families of 261 babies who had disappeared from hospitals took their cases to the attorney general. The first trial, of the doctor Eduardo Vela in 2018, ended in acquittal because the legal deadline for prosecution had passed. The 1977 Amnesty Law has hindered investigation, and many Women's Protection Board files went missing in 1996.

In 2023 the national Ombudsman, Ángel Gabilondo, presented Spain's first official inquiry into abuse by clergy. A survey of 8,000 adults done for the report found that 1.13 percent had been abused as children by clergy or lay church staff. Applied to the adult population, media put the number at about 440,000. Two months later an audit commissioned by the bishops counted at least 2,056 victims who were minors, and the bishops said it was "obvious that the number is higher".

In 2013 King Mohammed VI of Morocco pardoned 48 Spanish prisoners as a gesture towards Spain, among them Daniel Galván, who was serving 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children. The king revoked the pardon after protests, by which time Galván had left Morocco, and he was arrested in Spain and imprisoned there to finish his sentence.

The amnesty law and the lost files still hold back investigation of the children taken under Franco and afterwards. The church's own count of victims remains far below the figures drawn from the Ombudsman's survey.

GMB.story:
In 2003 The Gambia passed the Tourism Offences Act. It defines a child as anyone under 18, makes hotel operators liable if they knowingly allow child prostitution, and provides life imprisonment for child trafficking by tourists. In 2017 the US State Department, in its yearly report on human trafficking, said traffickers in The Gambia were increasingly hosting child sex tourists in private homes outside the commercial tourist areas, where the abuse was harder to detect.

The 2025 report says European tourists, mostly from the United Kingdom, reportedly travel to The Gambia to exploit children. Organized sex-trafficking networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country as a destination, especially the Senegambia Strip. Women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited for jobs in tourism and then sexually exploited.

The Gambia has also sent children abroad for adoption. After reports in 2019 of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia, the Flemish government in Belgium appointed an expert panel, which led to a review of every country Flemish families adopted from. As a result Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from The Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.

Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates of child sexual exploitation, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa lack representative survey data on abuse carried out through technology.

Tourists from Britain and elsewhere in Europe still travel to The Gambia to abuse children, and since at least 2017 some of it has moved into private homes. No survey exists that would show how many Gambian children are affected.

IMN.story:
From 1973 to 1983 Joseph Marshall and his wife ran Knottfield, a children's home owned by the Isle of Man Government. In 1992 Marshall was convicted of 13 offences relating to Knottfield.

In 2018 a scrutiny committee of Tynwald, the island's parliament, chaired by David Cretney, reported on the "horrific physical, emotional and sexual abuse" Marshall had committed at the home and made 11 recommendations. The report was withdrawn while a new criminal case against Marshall went ahead. In April 2022 he was jailed for six years for sexually abusing two boys at Knottfield. On 16 January 2023 the Isle of Man Government apologised for mistakes that had contributed to the abuse and said it supported all 11 recommendations.

The committee's report covers one home. No wider official inquiry into abuse in the island's institutions is recorded, so how far the failures at Knottfield happened elsewhere is not known.

ITA.story:
For decades juvenile courts and social services in Tuscany placed children at Il Forteto, a farming cooperative and community at Vicchio near Florence. Its founder, Rodolfo Fiesoli, already had a final conviction in 1985, and the placements continued. He was later sentenced to 14 years and 10 months for abuse. A parliamentary inquiry did not reach a final report, and in 2024 parliament created a new commission of inquiry to establish why the authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on abuse.

In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference, the body of Italy's Catholic bishops, said that under the Lateran concordat, the treaty between Italy and the Holy See, its priests had no obligation to report suspected abuse to the police. The priest Nicola Corradi, accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona in 2009, went on working at the order's school in Argentina, where he was convicted in 2019.

From 2022 the bishops' conference began publishing its own national reports. Its first counted 86 contacts to diocesan listening centres in 2020 and 2021, and its third, in 2025, counted 115 alleged victims in 2023 and 2024. Critics, including the victims' group Rete l'Abuso, said the reports leave out court and Vatican cases. In 2025 a Munich law firm hired by the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone found 59 victims in 67 cases since 1964 and called the diocese's handling of cases until 2010 a systemic failure.

Italy is also the destination for women and girls trafficked from Edo State in Nigeria, overland through Niger and Libya and then by boat. The UN migration agency recorded an almost 600 percent rise in potential victims arriving by sea between 2014 and 2017. In 2016 Europol said 5,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Italy, and that it had evidence some missing children in Europe had been sexually exploited.

Italy has held no national inquiry into abuse in its institutions as a whole, so the only national figures on church abuse are the ones the bishops publish about themselves.

LBR.story:
In 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, a court set up jointly by Sierra Leone and the UN, convicted Charles Taylor, a former president of Liberia, of aiding and abetting crimes committed by the Revolutionary United Front, a rebel force in Sierra Leone, including sexual slavery and the use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years.

In early 2002 a joint mission of the UN refugee agency and Save the Children UK reported that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by aid workers and peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN's internal investigators then examined 43 cases, substantiated 10, and said they found no evidence of "widespread" abuse. Under UN rules, only a peacekeeper's own country can prosecute him, so the UN can only send him home. In 2024 the UN still recorded two child victims linked to its Liberia mission, UNMIL.

After the civil war in Liberia ended in 2003, the number of private orphanages rose from 40 to 120. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed, and 89 of its 102 "orphans" were returned to their families. A 2007 report by UNICEF and the adoption agency Holt International found that many children entered the adoption process through fraud, including false promises to birth parents, and the UN mission found unaccredited orphanages run for profit. From 1994 to 2014 the United States issued 1,553 immigrant visas to children adopted from Monrovia, with a peak of 353 in 2006. Canada placed a moratorium on adoptions from Liberia.

Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates of child sexual exploitation, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa lack representative survey data on abuse carried out through technology.

Canada stopped adoptions from Liberia after the fraud was found. Children abused by peacekeepers there depend on the soldiers' own countries to bring charges, and how many Liberian children are abused online is not known.

MYS.story:
In November 2008 a team from Malaysia's Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development went to Sarawak to look into reports about Penan girls. The Penan are an indigenous people of Sarawak. Its report, made public in September 2009 after the Associated Press obtained it, found that workers of logging companies had raped or tried to sexually abuse Penan schoolgirls, some as young as 10. Some of the girls had been given lifts to school in logging trucks. The team named no company. Sarawak police said three complaints had been investigated the year before and none had been taken to court for lack of evidence.

In 2016 an undercover investigation by the Al Jazeera programme 101 East found babies advertised online with photos and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by gender, race and skin colour. It reported that some babies went to couples who wanted a child and others to traffickers. Among the mothers were immigrant sex workers who cannot legally bear children in Malaysia.

In September 2024 police raided 20 charity homes run by Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings, a company linked to the banned Al-Arqam religious movement, and arrested 171 adults. Police had received 41 reports about the group since 2011. By October they had rescued 625 children from its homes. Three student assistants at a religious school in Kuala Pilah were charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing five children, and police said the investigation pointed to organised crime and human trafficking.

Malaysia also hosts abuse material. The Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, acted on 17,046 internet addresses hosted in Malaysia in 2025, 5 percent of its total.

The Penan report named no company, and no prosecution of the loggers is recorded. The Global Ikhwan homes were raided in 2024 although police had received reports about the group since 2011, and servers in Malaysia still host 5 percent of the abuse material the Internet Watch Foundation acts on.

NZL.story:
The St John of God Brothers, a Catholic religious order, ran Marylands, a residential school in Christchurch for boys with learning disabilities. Of the 537 boys who attended, more than one in five reported abuse between 1955 and 1984, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served there and in Christchurch faced abuse allegations. After allegations against Brother Bernard McGrath in 1977, the order moved him to Australia. He was later put in charge of the order's Hebron Trust, where he abused youths, and he has been convicted of more than 100 offences in New Zealand and Australia.

From 1972 to 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit of Lake Alice, a state psychiatric hospital, and about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic given as punishment, and evidence was given that staff and adult patients raped children. The psychiatrist in charge, Selwyn Leeks, denied abuse and was never charged in New Zealand. In 2019 the UN Committee Against Torture found New Zealand had broken the Convention against Torture by failing to investigate properly.

The government set up the Confidential Listening and Assistance Service in 2008 to hear people abused in state care, and it heard 1,103 people before closing in 2015. A Royal Commission, a public inquiry with legal powers, followed from 2018. Its final report in July 2024 estimated that 200,000 of about 655,000 people in state and faith-based care between 1950 and 2019 were abused, and that Māori were more likely to be abused. It found that the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse and that the Catholic Church, on the advice of psychiatrists, had moved abusers to other ministries, where they abused again. In December 2024 the government apologised for the torture at Lake Alice and offered each survivor NZ$150,000.

The Royal Commission made 138 recommendations and found that by 2024 very little progress had been made on the redress system it proposed in 2021. It recommended an investigation into priests sent to Papua New Guinea after abuse allegations.

SLE.story:
During Sierra Leone's civil war, from 1991 to 2002, armed groups abducted girls and held them as sexual slaves. In 2004 the country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that two of these groups, the rebel Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), had "deliberately embarked on systematic strategies to abduct and rape women and girls between the ages of ten and 14 years". The girls were used as sexual and domestic slaves and as "wives". Of 189 allegations of sexual slavery made to the commission, 72.5 percent were attributed to the RUF. The commission also found that the Civil Defence Forces carried out a deliberate strategy of rape against girls, and that girls as young as 12 were forced to pay for aid with sex.

The Special Court for Sierra Leone, set up jointly by the country and the UN, tried leaders of the armed groups. In 2009 it convicted three RUF leaders, Issa Sesay, Morris Kallon and Augustine Gbao, of sexual slavery and of forced marriage, the first forced-marriage convictions by an international criminal court, and sentenced them to 52, 40 and 25 years. In 2012 it convicted Charles Taylor, a former president of Liberia, of aiding the RUF's crimes, including the use of children under 15 as fighters, and sentenced him to 50 years.

In 1998 about 29 children at a centre in Makeni run by the charity Help A Needy Child International (HANCI) were taken to Freetown for medical checks and never returned. Their parents later learned that Americans had adopted them. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions in 2009, and in 2012 a presidential commission closed HANCI and found that the families "cannot be said to have genuinely consented".

Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates of child sexual exploitation, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa lack representative survey data on abuse carried out through technology.

Leaders of the RUF and Charles Taylor were convicted and jailed, and adoptions from Sierra Leone have been suspended since 2009. No survey shows how many children in Sierra Leone are abused online.

TCD.story:
In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were stopped in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to host families in France. The charity said the children were orphans from Darfur in neighbouring Sudan. The Chadian authorities found that most were from Chad and were not orphans. In December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour. They were transferred to France, and in March 2008 Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them.

Chadian soldiers have also been accused of abusing children abroad, and the UN has verified abuse by them at home. Between December 2013 and June 2014, boys sheltering at the M'Poko camp in Bangui, in the Central African Republic, said soldiers had sexually abused them, often in exchange for food or money. Most of the soldiers they described were from the French Sangaris force, and some were Chadian and Equatorial Guinean troops of MISCA, an African peacekeeping force. In 2015 an independent panel appointed by the UN Secretary-General called the UN's handling of the reports a "gross institutional failure". In 2022 the UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province, and in Sudan it attributed 4 of 35 cases of sexual violence against girls to the same army. It also verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and Diffa, in the Lake Chad basin.

Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates of child sexual exploitation, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa lack representative survey data on abuse carried out through technology.

The Zoé's Ark members were pardoned within a few months of their conviction. Abuse of girls by Chad's own army was still being verified by the UN in 2022, and no survey shows how many Chadian children are abused online.

VNM.story:
In April 1975 children were airlifted out of Vietnam in Operation Babylift, and a later lawsuit alleged that many of them were not orphans. Adoptions abroad continued in the following decades, and from 1994 to 2014 the United States alone issued 7,498 immigrant visas to children adopted from Hanoi, with a peak of 828 in 2007.

In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi reported that the number of babies recorded as abandoned had risen 17-fold or more at orphanages in seven provinces. Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the United States when it expired that September. In 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and doctors and nurses at village clinics, for abuse of power. They were accused of asking poor families for their infants and falsifying documents to say the babies had been abandoned, and 266 babies were sent abroad for adoption between 2005 and 2008. Vietnam still sent 14,039 children abroad between 2003 and 2022, and in Belgium the Flemish government later stopped adoptions from Vietnam.

Foreigners also came to Vietnam to abuse children. In 2007 an Australian charity found 80 commercial cases of child exploitation by foreigners in Sa Pa, and the same year Vietnam set up a unit in the Ministry of Public Security to investigate child sex tourism. In 2006 a Vietnamese court had convicted the British singer Paul Gadd, known as Gary Glitter, of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11.

Vietnamese children are also trafficked out of the country. The 2025 US State Department report on trafficking says traffickers in border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriages, and Vietnam identified 236 child victims in 2024. In Britain, 416 Vietnamese children were referred as potential victims of modern slavery that year, and Vietnamese children and adults there are exploited on cannabis farms and in nail salons.

Adoption from Vietnam has been cut back after the fraud cases. Vietnamese girls continue to be trafficked to China, and Vietnamese children to Britain.
